overview: This long map record spans Anglo-Egyptian colonial rule, Sudan’s independence in 1956 and later upheavals. It also contains a border error: South Sudan became a separate country in 2011, although the imported shape continues to include it. Sudan’s history includes irrigation, medical education, literature and community organization as well as conflict.

periods.title: Colonial institutions and Sudanese initiatives
periods.summary: Irrigation projects and new training institutions developed within an unequal colonial system.

periods.title: Independence and civil wars
periods.summary: Independent Sudan experienced prolonged conflict; the 2005 peace agreement led towards the southern referendum.

periods.title: Separation and contested political futures
periods.summary: South Sudan separated in 2011; Sudan’s later civilian transition was interrupted by a coup and war.

items.text: The Sennar Dam was completed in 1925 on the Blue Nile, helping supply the Gezira irrigation scheme between the Blue and White Niles. Canals carried water into agricultural land, connecting a major engineering project with the timing and work of farming.

Gezira’s organization divided responsibilities between government, the managing company and tenant farmers. Cotton linked the scheme with commercial markets, while sorghum and forage crops also appeared in crop rotations. Behind the canals were negotiations about labour, management and returns.

Khartoum’s Kitchener School of Medicine opened on 29 February 1924 and used Khartoum Hospital for teaching. Its first course lasted four years, with a small intake. Students learned in a working medical institution as well as in classrooms.

Ali Bedri was among the 1928 graduates and later held senior hospital posts and became minister of health. Sudanese graduates developed medical services and public institutions. The school eventually became part of the University of Khartoum.

The Midwifery Training School opened in Omdurman in 1921. Its history brings childbirth and women’s professional knowledge into the picture of colonial medicine, alongside hospitals and male doctors. Training involved negotiation with existing practitioners and local social life.

sections.title: Women’s education and an Arabic title

items.text: Ahfad’s educational roots reach back to Babiker Badri’s girls’ school at Rufa’a in 1907. Later intermediate and secondary schools preceded the women’s college of 1966. This was a sustained Sudanese educational initiative across several generations.

Ahfad’s Rural Extension Program began in 1973 and became required in 1978. Students worked with rural communities through field learning, research and service. Learning could mean listening to a community’s priorities far from a lecture hall.

“موسم الهجرة الى الشمال” is the Arabic title of Tayeb Salih’s novel, known in English as “Season of Migration to the North”. This sample follows the spelling in a library catalogue for a 1997 edition; the novel was first published in 1966.

Salih’s novel follows a young man returning to a Sudanese village after studying abroad. Its movement between places helped make questions of colonialism, home and identity part of an internationally read Sudanese literary achievement.

sections.title: Political change and keeping daily life going

items.text: South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011 after a referendum. This was a major change in the territory of Sudan. The two countries have separate histories after that date, even when an imported map polygon fails to separate them.

A transition towards civilian rule began in 2019, but a military coup in October 2021 interrupted it. Fighting between rival armed forces erupted in April 2023. These changes deeply affected civilians’ ability to stay at home, work and attend school.

UNDP’s 2025 account describes women-led community kitchens serving people displaced by war alongside host communities. Organizing ingredients, cooking and sharing meals became part of local emergency action. Neighbours helped sustain daily life under extremely difficult conditions.

UNICEF’s 2025 reporting describes health facilities and mobile teams continuing emergency care in conflict-affected areas. Keeping services operating depended on people, supplies and routes that could still be reached. The report records relief work within an ongoing crisis.

ending.text: Sudan continues as a country; its peoples have not vanished amid war or political rupture. South Sudan separated in 2011. The civilian transition and conflict beginning in 2023 belong to an unresolved recent history, while community organizations continue working to sustain lives.
